data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is best explained by the reduced sky view factor in dense urban street canyons, which traps outgoing longwave radiation, and the gap is larger in cities with taller buildings and narrower streets.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If urban geometry features wide streets and low building height, the sky view factor approaches that of the countryside, neutralizing the radiation trap.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If atmospheric moisture or cloud cover raises baseline longwave downwelling uniformly, the relative disadvantage of a low sky view factor is diminished.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Outgoing longwave radiation from urban surfaces is partially absorbed and re-emitted by building walls, reducing the effective sky view factor and trapping heat within the street canyon. This steric obstruction of radiative cooling prevents the urban surface from shedding heat as efficiently as the open countryside. Consequently, the night-time gap scales with building height and built density, which lower the sky view factor and enhance longwave trapping.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
